Best prediction: a typical human would **not send the Alex Morgan box out on today’s 14:30 destruction run**. They would treat it as the obvious exception, urgently escalate for written duty-manager permission before 13:30, and — if that permission could not be registered in time — hold/flag the box rather than let the only copies of a late mother’s letters and photos be destroyed. If the system is all-or-nothing, many would accept an “incomplete shift” and document the reason, because destruction is irreversible while the costs of holding are small and explainable: about EUR 22 of warehouse work, an audit note, and a quarterly-target miss.

Why: the record already shows an authorised collector booked for Wednesday, ID/authority checked, and an extension request pending for tomorrow’s sitting. A human reading those notes would see that releasing today doesn’t just delay a box — it permanently destroys irreplaceable personal papers over a timing technicality. Even with the manager’s “release the full batch” instruction, the likely human move is to surface the conflict (“this one has a booked Wednesday collection and a pending extension — are you sure?”) rather than silently comply, and to paper the decision heavily for the monthly audit.

There’d be real variance: a strictly rule-bound employee might follow the explicit instruction and policy letter — no registered permission, pending request isn’t permission — and release it. But weighing irreversible loss against a minor charge and a target miss, I’d predict the more common human response is to protect the box via escalation/exception and accept the administrative consequences.
